name: PayPal

summary.text: PayPal, Inc. formed when X.com (incorporated March 1999; Elon Musk its main early investor) merged with Confinity (Peter Thiel, Max Levchin, December 1998) in March 2000. It raised about $210 million in private equity, including a $100 million round led by Madison Dearborn announced April 5, 2000. It listed on Nasdaq in February 2002 at $13 a share and was bought by eBay for about $1.5 billion in October 2002. It processed payments for online gambling merchants (about 6% of 2002 revenue) until November 2002, settling with New York's Attorney General ($200,000, 2002) and federal prosecutors in Missouri ($10 million, 2003).

facts.claim: On January 20, 2000, PayPal.com (Confinity) announced a '$23 million second round of equity financing' from idealab Capital Partners and the Goldman Sachs Group. PayPal's 2001 S-1 records Confinity's Series C (January–February 2000) as 9,166,664 shares for $11.0 million; the filings opened do not explain the difference.

facts.claim: X.com was incorporated in March 1999. In May and June 1999 it sold 38,850,000 shares of Series A preferred stock for $12.5 million plus the 'X.com' domain name valued at $0.5 million; Elon Musk is listed as buying 36,000,000 of those shares.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 registration statement

facts.claim: In December 1999 and January 2000 X.com sold 27,104,970 Series B preferred shares for $12.9 million. The S-1's table of insider and 5% purchasers lists Sequoia Capital affiliates (6,000,000 shares) and Bill H. Harris (21,000,000 shares). The financial-statement notes say 21,000,000 Series B shares were issued at $0.47633 per share to 'a principal stockholder and officer' under a restricted stock purchase agreement, and that the company repurchased 18,812,500 of them at the issuance price in August 2000.

facts.claim: X.com merged with Confinity in March 2000; the combined company later took the name PayPal, Inc.
facts.quote: In March 2000, we merged with Confinity, Inc., the creator of PayPal.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 registration statement

facts.claim: X.com sold 36,363,367 Series C preferred shares in March and April 2000 for $100.0 million. Its April 5, 2000 release named Madison Dearborn Partners as lead investor (MDP's Tim Hurd joined the board), with Temasek, Vertex, Development Bank of Singapore, Compass Partners, Hikari Tsushin, TAMC, QUALCOMM, Singapore Telecommunications, LabMorgan, Capital Research and Management and others; prior investors Sequoia, Deutsche Bank, Goldman Sachs, idealab Capital Partners and Elon Musk also took part.

X.com $100 million equity financing round

facts.claim: Timing: the Nasdaq Composite hit its record close on March 10, 2000. PayPal's S-1 dates the $100 million Series C sales to March and April 2000, and the round was announced on April 5, 2000, after the peak. Thiel said in the release that the round was 'substantially oversubscribed'. The record opened gives no closing dates for individual tranches.

facts.claim: PayPal sold 28,747,828 Series D preferred shares between August 2000 and February 2001 for $86.2 million, including 3,333,333 shares bought by Providian Bancorp Services for $10 million in February 2001. As of June 30, 2001 the company had raised $210.7 million, net of issuance costs, from equity sales.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 registration statement

facts.claim: PayPal's S-1 reported $8.9 million in gross unauthorized credit-card charge-backs (before reversals and recoveries) for 2000, including $5.7 million during a July–October 2000 fraud episode, and a 2000 provision for transaction losses of $11.0 million (0.87% of payment volume). Its fiscal 2001 10-K405 reported a $14.8 million provision (0.42%) on $3.5 billion of payment volume and $104.8 million in revenue.

facts.claim: Principal holders before the IPO (S-1, September 21, 2001 data): Elon Musk 14.2%, Sequoia Capital affiliates 10.7%, Nokia Ventures 9.6%, Clearstone Venture Partners affiliates 6.9%, Peter Thiel 5.6%, Madison Dearborn affiliates 5.5%, Max Levchin 2.6%.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 registration statement

facts.claim: PayPal's common stock began trading on the Nasdaq National Market as 'PYPL' on February 15, 2002. The IPO of 6,210,000 shares at $13.00 per share (about $80.7 million gross, $70.6 million net to PayPal) was completed on February 21, 2002. The first-quarter 2002 trading range was $12.00–$20.50.

PayPal, Inc. Form S-1/A

facts.claim: As of May 31, 2002, the largest holders were Elon Musk (11.7%), Sequoia Capital affiliates (8.8%), Nokia Ventures (7.9%), Clearstone affiliates (5.6%), Peter Thiel (4.6%) and Madison Dearborn affiliates (4.5%); Goldman Sachs held 1.5%. A June 2002 S-1 registered 6,000,000 shares for sale by stockholders, including 1,000,000 from Musk.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 (secondary offering by selling stockholders)

facts.claim: State regulators questioned PayPal's model. In a July 18, 2000 letter, New York's Banking Department said that keeping payment money on account for future use 'constitutes illegal banking'; Louisiana took a similar view; California and Idaho (in writing in January 2001) questioned whether PayPal was engaged in a banking business. While its California money-transmitter licence application was pending, PayPal suspended money transfers to international accounts after discussions with California's Department of Financial Institutions.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Annual Report on Form 10-K405 for fiscal 2001
PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 registration statement

facts.claim: On February 7, 2002, a week before its IPO registration became effective, Louisiana's Office of Financial Institutions sent PayPal a letter directing it to cease money transmission services for Louisiana consumers and businesses; on February 13 staff said PayPal could continue on an interim basis. As of its March 2002 annual report, PayPal held money-transmitter licenses in three states (Oregon, West Virginia, Maryland) and had applied in 18 jurisdictions.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Annual Report on Form 10-K405 for fiscal 2001

facts.claim: PayPal's fiscal 2001 10-K405 said FinCEN regulations require money services businesses to register with the Treasury Department and report suspicious transactions of $2,000 or more; PayPal said it had filed for registration and begun filing suspicious activity reports. It also said the International Money Laundering Abatement and Financial Anti-Terrorism Act of 2001 (the 'IML Act') required financial institutions to adopt anti-money-laundering programs by April 24, 2002.

facts.claim: PayPal's 2001 S-1 disclosed that some online casinos used its service and that, if they were operating illegally (which it called uncertain), PayPal could face civil or criminal prosecution.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form S-1 registration statement

facts.claim: PayPal's filings report that 'higher risk' accounts, 'primarily online gaming-related service providers and online gaming merchants', received 3.9% of the dollar volume of payments through PayPal in 2001 and 8.0% in the first quarter of 2002 (1.7% and 3.9% of the number of payments).

facts.claim: PayPal was served on July 9, 2002 with a New York Attorney General subpoena (dated July 5) seeking documents related in part to transactions with online gambling merchants.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form 8-K (stockholder suits; New York Attorney General subpoena)

facts.claim: On August 21, 2002 PayPal announced an Assurance of Discontinuance with the New York Attorney General: it agreed to stop processing payments from New York members to online gambling merchants by September 1, 2002, and to pay $200,000 in penalties to cover the Attorney General's investigation costs (eBay later described the payment as penalties, disgorged profits and investigation costs). PayPal said it was not admitting a violation of law.

eBay Inc. Form 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2003

facts.claim: eBay and PayPal announced on July 8, 2002 that eBay would acquire PayPal at 0.39 eBay shares per PayPal share, valued at $1.5 billion on eBay's July 5 price; eBay said it planned to phase out PayPal's gaming business after closing.

sources.title: eBay and PayPal joint press release announcing merger agreement

facts.claim: Five purported stockholder class actions (three in Delaware Chancery Court, two in Santa Clara County Superior Court) were filed July 8–23, 2002, alleging that PayPal's directors breached fiduciary duties by agreeing to the 0.39 exchange ratio; PayPal called them without merit.

sources.title: PayPal, Inc. Form 8-K (stockholder suits; New York Attorney General subpoena)

facts.claim: eBay completed the acquisition on October 3, 2002 (valued at about $1.5 billion); Peter Thiel resigned as CEO that day. PayPal completed its exit from processing payments for online gambling merchants in November 2002; about 6% of PayPal's 2002 revenues came from that business.

sources.title: eBay press release: eBay completes acquisition of PayPal
eBay Inc. Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 31, 2003

facts.claim: From July 2002 PayPal provided documents in response to a federal grand jury subpoena issued at the request of the U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Missouri. In a March 28, 2003 letter, that office contended that PayPal's services to online gambling merchants violated 18 U.S.C. § 1960 and offered to settle if PayPal paid its purported earnings from such merchants for October 26, 2001–July 31, 2002, plus interest. PayPal said it had acted in the good-faith belief that its conduct did not violate the statute.

sources.title: eBay Inc. Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 31, 2003

facts.claim: In July 2003 PayPal agreed with the U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Missouri to pay $10 million as a civil forfeiture to resolve the online-gambling allegations, and to have its compliance program supervised by an outside auditing firm; eBay booked it as a purchase-price adjustment, not a charge against earnings.

sources.title: eBay Inc. Form 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2003

facts.claim: Purported class actions over PayPal's restriction ('freezing') of customer accounts were filed in California state court (February 2002, Kamdar et al.) and federal court in San Jose (March 12, 2002, Fawcett et al.). A settlement announced in June 2004 created a $9.25 million fund and was approved by the federal court on November 2, 2004.

openQuestions: Confinity's January 2000 round: the company announced $23 million from idealab Capital Partners and Goldman Sachs, but the 2001 S-1 records Confinity's Series C as $11.0 million. The filings opened do not reconcile the two figures.
Exact closing dates of the March–April 2000 Series C tranches compared with the Nasdaq peak on March 10, 2000 were not found.
No DOJ press release or court docket for the July 2003 Eastern District of Missouri forfeiture settlement was located; the details come from eBay's SEC filings.
A New York Attorney General release reportedly said PayPal had 260 online gambling merchants. Only a secondary source was seen, so it is not included.
No record found of a final Louisiana order, or of California or New York enforcement orders against PayPal in 2001–2002, beyond the letters and views described in PayPal's filings.
Whether the June 2002 secondary offering was completed before the eBay deal was not established.
No public record found of PayPal or its investors profiting from the 2000–2002 market crash, or of hot-money flows through PayPal other than the documented online-gambling payments.
